name: Dune Palimpsest
description: Dune Palimpsest is a small desert world whose surface has been written and overwritten by successive eras of climate change. Dead riverbeds cut across dust seas, their courses tracing the paths of water that flowed when the atmosphere was thicker and the sun closer. Ancient ocean basins, now filled with fine sand, still bear the mineral tide-marks of their former shores. An impact crater at the equator has become the planet's deepest dust basin, its bowl filling and emptying with the shifting sands in cycles that geologists use as a rough clock.

The low gravity gives the sand a peculiar behavior—dust devils grow to extraordinary heights, spiraling kilometers into the thin sky before dissipating, and sand dunes migrate visibly over the course of days. Flora survives in the deepest riverbeds, where subsurface moisture still seeps through ancient aquifers: tough, dormant root systems that send up brief sprays of grey-green growth during the rare moisture cycles. These plants represent the last vestiges of a biosphere that once covered the entire planet.

A terraforming attempt was made here eighty years ago, aimed at restoring the atmosphere and reactivating the water cycle. The equipment—atmospheric processors and water extraction rigs—was deployed across the equatorial band but failed within a decade when the energy costs proved unsustainable and the atmospheric processors succumbed to sand infiltration. The abandoned equipment now stands half-buried in the dunes, slowly being overwritten by the same desert forces it was meant to overcome.

Dune Palimpsest's remaining flora is endangered by the continued drying of the subsurface aquifers, a process the failed terraforming may have accelerated by disrupting the natural water table. Conservation biologists have proposed a more modest intervention—maintaining the aquifer levels rather than attempting full terraforming—but the remoteness of the world makes even this limited effort expensive. The planet continues its slow erasure, each layer of sand burying the traces of what came before, a palimpsest that will eventually be scraped clean to bare stone.
